paras: The lynching of John Boggs took place on the night of 18 March 1880, when about one hundred regulators raided James Binion's house on Upper Big Sinking Creek in Carter County, Kentucky, shot Binion dead and hanged Boggs from a tree in the yard. Dispatches from Grayson carried the story across the country within days, and in 1882 a Detroit Free Press feature retold it, with the roles of the two men reversed, as part of a history of the Kentucky Regulators.

In October 1879 about 200 regulators had ridden into Martinsburg, the seat of neighboring Elliott County, taken John W. Kendall and William McMillan from the jail and hanged them on a walnut tree. George W. Symonds's 1882 feature traced the order to citizens' meetings called after a store was robbed and burned in 1877, and said it had set out to break up a gang of thieves and counterfeiters led by Peter J. Livingstone of Cracker's Neck. According to the feature, the Regulators' lodge sentenced Kendall, McMillan, Livingstone, Lewis Binion, John Binion and John Boggs to death.

According to the Courier-Journal's Grayson correspondent, the party went to Binion's house to notify Boggs, described as "a notorious character" who was hiding there, to leave the county. Binion refused to open the door and fired about fifty shots at the regulators, killing one of them, "it is believed." The regulators then broke down the doors and killed Binion with three shots, while a rock thrown at the door broke his wife's right leg.

After what the Cincinnati Gazette's dispatch called a "short trial," they took Boggs to a walnut tree fifteen steps from the house, hanged him with a cotton rope and fired two shots into his body. Before leaving they whipped Binion's nineteen-year-old son for joining in the firing.

A Dr. Steel found Boggs hanging the next morning, cut the rope and took the body to his family. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and the 1882 feature said that no effort had been made to bring the Regulators to justice for the Martinsburg hangings.

Two separate Grayson dispatches, one to the Louisville Courier-Journal and one to the Cincinnati Gazette, ran in papers from Washington and Richmond to Dallas, Cheyenne and Salt Lake City between 20 and 25 March 1880. Most printed them as short items that repeated the regulators' account that they had come only to warn Boggs off, though headlines varied from the Richmond Dispatch's "A Notorious Character Lynched in Kentucky" to the Evening Star's "Another Kentucky Outrage." The Fayette County Herald in Ohio called the party "the mob," while the Stark County Democrat headed the fullest account "A Fierce and Fatal Conflict and Lynching."

Symonds's "The Romance of Cracker's Neck" appeared in the Detroit Free Press early in 1882 and was reprinted in The Bee in June and the Mineral Point Tribune in July. It praised the Regulators for having "restored order and made law respected" while describing the hanging at length, and no paper in either period named the race of anyone involved.

The 1882 feature told a different story: John Binion and Boggs, both under sentence, met at a log cabin Boggs used when hunting in order to flee the county, and when they refused to surrender the Regulators shot Boggs dead and hanged the wounded Binion from the nearest tree. The two 1880 dispatches, written from Grayson the day after the raid, agree with each other that Binion was shot in his own house and Boggs was the one hanged, and they are the closer evidence. The feature also described a separate killing, the hanging of Louis Binion to a ladder at his own house the night after the Martinsburg lynching.
